title: 07. Google ADK: Day 6 — AgentTool, McpToolset & Pre-built Tools
summary: Wrap agents as tools, plug into the Model Context Protocol, and reach for ADK's built-in toolbox
objectives: Architecture — Where tools fit in the ADK stack

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Wrap agents as tools, plug into the Model Context Protocol, and reach for ADK's built-in toolbox

Day 6 / 15
ADK v2.7.0 (Aug 2026)
Python 3.10+

🎯 Learning Objectives

- Wrap one agent as a callable tool for another using `AgentTool` — and know when to prefer it over `sub_agents`

- Connect ADK to any MCP server via `McpToolset` using stdio and streamable-HTTP transports

- Whitelist tools with `tool_filter` and exploit v2.7.0's `elicitation_callback` support

- Reach for ADK's pre-built toolbox: `google_search`, `load_memory`, `load_web_page`, `OpenApiToolset`, `BuiltInCodeExecutor`, and friends

- Reason about control flow, plugin inheritance, and grounding-metadata propagation when composing tools

sections.title: 1. Why this matters
sections.body:
Real agents do not live in isolation. A customer-support agent needs to summarize chat transcripts, look up shipping status from a third-party logistics API, search the live web for recall notices, and consult a coding sub-agent to interpret stack traces — all in the same turn. If you had to hand-roll every integration, you would never ship.

Day 06 is about **plumbing**: how ADK lets you compose capabilities without writing glue code. There are three orthogonal axes you must learn:

1. **Agent-as-a-Tool** — wrap an entire `LlmAgent` as a single tool on another agent's `tools=[...]` list. The parent calls it like any function, gets back text, and keeps going. This is *focused delegation*: the parent stays in control.
2. **McpToolset** — consume the entire [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) ecosystem. One class gives your agent read_file, list_directory, GitHub issues, Slack messages, Postgres queries — anything an MCP server exposes — with no Python wrappers on your side.
3. **Pre-built tools** — ADK ships with batteries: `google_search` for live grounding, `load_memory` for cross-session recall, `load_web_page` for HTML fetch-and-summarize, `OpenApiToolset` for any REST API documented with an OpenAPI spec, `BuiltInCodeExecutor` for sandboxed Python, plus Vertex AI Search, Discovery Engine, and the new stable `DataAgentToolset`.

By the end of today, you will be able to drop a `McpToolset` into a 5-line agent and immediately have 15 file-system tools, ship a `google_search`-backed news agent in under a minute, and know exactly when an `AgentTool` is preferable to a `sub_agents=[...]` declaration. These are the load-bearing primitives behind every non-trivial ADK deployment.

sections.title: 2. Core Concepts
sections.body:
Four building blocks: AgentTool, McpToolset, the pre-built tool catalog, and a decision matrix for choosing between them.

### 2.1 AgentTool — wrap one agent as another agent's tool

`AgentTool` lives at `google.adk.tools.agent_tool.AgentTool` and is also re-exported from `google.adk.tools`. You construct it with a child `LlmAgent` and add it to the parent's `tools` list like any other callable:

```python
from google.adk.tools.agent_tool import AgentTool
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent

summary_agent = Agent(name="summarizer", model="gemini-2.0-flash",
                      instruction="Summarize the input text in 3 bullets.")
root_agent = Agent(
    name="parent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction="Use the summarizer tool for any text the user wants summarized.",
    tools=[AgentTool(agent=summary_agent, skip_summarization=True)],
)
```

When the parent's LLM decides to call the AgentTool, ADK runs the child agent to completion, takes its final text, and returns it as the function response — exactly as if a Python tool had returned a `dict`. Control then **returns to the parent**, which may keep calling other tools or produce its own final response.

**Fields worth knowing:**
- `agent` (required) — the wrapped `LlmAgent`.
- `skip_summarization` (default `False`) — pass `True` to skip the parent's "summarize the tool result" LLM pass. Recommended when the child already produces polished output.
- `include_plugins` (default `True`) — child inherits the parent's `plugins` list. Set `False` if the child needs a clean plugin stack (e.g. an audit plugin that should only see parent calls).
- `propagate_grounding_metadata` — forward Google Search grounding citations from the child to the parent's response. Use when the child uses `google_search` and you want citations surfaced in the parent's reply.

**Versus `sub_agents=[...]`:** sub-agents are a *transfer* mechanism — the user is routed to the child, who owns the rest of the turn. AgentTool is a *tool call* — the parent stays in charge. If the parent needs the child's *output*, use AgentTool. If the child should take over the conversation, use sub-agents.

```
AGENT-AS-A-TOOL  vs  SUB-AGENT
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  AgentTool  (control RETURNS to parent)
  ─────────────────────────────────────
       ┌───────────────┐
       │ parent_agent  │
       └───────┬───────┘
               │ calls AgentTool (summarizer_agent)
               ▼
       ┌───────────────┐
       │ summarizer    │  runs to completion
       │ (AgentTool)   │  returns text → tool response
       └───────┬───────┘
               │ tool result back to parent's LLM
               ▼
       ┌───────────────┐
       │ parent_agent  │  ← continues SAME turn, may call more tools
       │ (LLM resumes) │     or produce final response
       └───────────────┘

  Sub-agent  (control TRANSFERS to child, child ends turn)
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       ┌───────────────┐
       │ parent_agent  │
       └───────┬───────┘
               │ transfer_to_agent('weather_agent')
               ▼
       ┌───────────────┐
       │ weather_agent │  takes over, owns the rest of the turn
       └───────┬───────┘
               │ final response to user
               ▼
              END

  Rule of thumb:
   • Use AgentTool     when parent needs the child's OUTPUT, then continues
   • Use sub_agents    when child should OWN the conversation from here on
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

💡 Key Concept

`include_plugins=True` means a `BigQueryAgentAnalyticsPlugin` on the parent will *also* fire when the child agent runs. This is usually what you want (one audit trail), but it doubles plugin cost. Set `include_plugins=False` to give the child an isolated plugin stack.

### 2.2 McpToolset — the Model Context Protocol bridge

[MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) is an open JSON-RPC protocol that standardizes how LLMs discover and invoke external tools. An *MCP server* exposes a list of tools; an *MCP client* (your ADK agent) calls them. The protocol supports resources (read-only data) and prompts (parameterized templates), but ADK focuses on tools.

ADK's `McpToolset` at `google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.McpToolset` is a single class that supports **two transports**:

**Stdio (local subprocess).** Spawn a local MCP server as a child process; communicate over its stdin/stdout. The canonical example is Anthropic's filesystem server:

```python
from mcp import StdioServerParameters
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool import McpToolset
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.mcp_session_manager import StdioConnectionParams

fs_toolset = McpToolset(
    connection_params=StdioConnectionParams(
        server_params=StdioServerParameters(
            command="npx",
            args=["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem",
                  "/ABSOLUTE/PATH/TO/FOLDER"],
        ),
    ),
    tool_filter=["list_directory", "read_file"],  # whitelist
)
```

**Streamable HTTP (remote).** Connect to a remote MCP endpoint over HTTP with optional SSE streaming. The official Google Maps Grounding Lite server is the textbook example:

```python
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.mcp_session_manager import StreamableHTTPConnectionParams

maps_toolset = McpToolset(
    connection_params=StreamableHTTPConnectionParams(
        url="https://mapstools.googleapis.com/mcp",
        headers={
            "X-Goog-Api-Key": GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY,
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
            "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream",
        },
    ),
)
```

Both transports yield the same `McpToolset` object — your agent code is transport-agnostic. Under the hood, ADK uses [FastMCP](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) for protocol handling.

**Key methods:** `get_tools()` (called by the Runner on first invocation — actually opens the MCP session and lists tools), `close()` (tear down subprocess or HTTP stream — call at shutdown), `list_resources()`, `read_resource(uri)`, `get_resource_info(uri)`.

**v2.7.0 additions:** `McpToolset` can now *reuse* an MCP server's existing tool list without re-fetching (perf win for hot-reload dev loops), and supports an `elicitation_callback` — a Python callable invoked when the MCP server requests additional information from the user mid-tool-call (e.g. an OAuth consent prompt).

```
MCP TOOLSET LIFECYCLE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Agent boots
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ McpToolset(connection_params)│  ← build toolset (no I/O yet)
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │  Runner calls get_tools() on first invocation
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ launch MCP server (npx or    │  Stdio → spawn subprocess
  │ HTTP GET to /mcp endpoint)   │  HTTP → open SSE/streaming session
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │  tools/list  →  list of tool definitions
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Apply tool_filter whitelist  │  e.g. ['list_directory','read_file']
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │  inject surviving tools into Agent.tools
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ LLM calls tool → tool call   │  McpToolset.run_async(...)
  │ forwarded to MCP server via  │  tools/call JSON-RPC
  │ the active MCP session       │
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │  tool result returned as function_response
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Runner closes toolset at     │  McpToolset.close() kills subprocess
  │ session shutdown / exit      │  or terminates HTTP stream
  └──────────────────────────────┘
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

⚠️ Important

**MCP subprocesses do not play well with `adk web --reload` on Windows.** The reloader kills the parent process, which orphans the npx subprocess. Use `adk web --no-reload` on Windows when working with stdio MCP servers, or do MCP work via `adk run` / `adk api_server` instead.

### 2.3 ADK's pre-built tool catalog

ADK ships with a toolbox of first-party tools you can drop into any agent. None require external subprocesses; all live in `google.adk.tools` (or sibling modules).

| Tool | Import | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `google_search` | `from google.adk.tools import google_search` | Grounds the LLM response on the live Google Search index. Returns grounding metadata with citations the LLM can quote. |
| `load_memory` | `from google.adk.tools import load_memory` | Auto-injected tool that queries the configured `MemoryService`. Use when the agent should recall facts from past sessions. |
| `load_web_page` | `from google.adk.tools import load_web_page` | Fetches a URL, strips HTML, returns markdown-ish text. Cheaper than `google_search` for known URLs. |
| `BuiltInCodeExecutor` | `from google.adk.code_executors import BuiltInCodeExecutor` | Sandboxed Python execution. The LLM writes code, ADK runs it, the result feeds back. |
| `OpenApiToolset` | `from google.adk.tools.openapi_tool import OpenApiToolset` | Generates FunctionTools from any OpenAPI 3.x spec — point at a URL or local file, get a fully typed toolset. |
| `VertexAiSearchTool` | `from google.adk.tools.vertex_ai_search_tool import VertexAiSearchTool` | Queries a Vertex AI Search app for grounding over your private corpus. |
| `DiscoveryEngineSearchTool` | `from google.adk.tools.discovery_engine_search_tool import DiscoveryEngineSearchTool` | Lower-level Discovery Engine search (the API under Vertex AI Search). |
| `DataAgentToolset` | `from google.adk.tools import DataAgentToolset` | **Stable in v2.7.0.** BigQuery / SQL natural-language querying with schema awareness. |
| `transfer_to_agent` | `from google.adk.tools import transfer_to_agent` | Hand control to another agent by name. The primitive that powers `sub_agents`. |
| `exit_loop` | `from google.adk.tools import exit_loop` | Terminate a `LoopAgent` early. Used inside loop bodies. |
| `LoadArtifactsTool` | `from google.adk.tools.load_artifacts_tool import LoadArtifactsTool` | Loads a saved artifact (file) into context on demand. |

**`google_search` deserves special mention.** It is the easiest way to give your agent current information — no API key beyond your Gemini key, no MCP setup. Just `tools=[google_search]` and the LLM will ground its answers on the live web, returning a `grounding_metadata` block you can render as inline citations. We will use it in Example 4.

**`OpenApiToolset` is the secret weapon** for third-party REST APIs. Hand it any OpenAPI 3 spec — Stripe, GitHub, your internal billing service — and you get a typed toolset for free. We will not build a full example today (it deserves its own treatment), but the exercise section challenges you to wire one up.

🚀 Pro Tip

`google_search` and `BuiltInCodeExecutor` are zero-config — just add them to `tools`. But `OpenApiToolset`, `VertexAiSearchTool`, and `DataAgentToolset` require service-account or API-key setup; do not assume they "just work" on day one of a project.

### 2.4 Decision matrix — which tool wrapper to reach for

When you have a capability to expose, here is the decision tree:

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| You have a Python function | `FunctionTool` (or just put the function in `tools=[...]`) |
| You have a child LlmAgent whose **output** the parent needs | `AgentTool(agent=child, skip_summarization=True)` |
| You have a child LlmAgent that should **take over** the conversation | `sub_agents=[child]` (the framework auto-injects `transfer_to_agent`) |
| You want a public MCP server's tools (filesystem, GitHub, Slack, Postgres) | `McpToolset` with `StdioConnectionParams` |
| You want a remote HTTP MCP server (Google Maps, your own FastMCP server) | `McpToolset` with `StreamableHTTPConnectionParams` |
| You want live web grounding | `google_search` |
| You want to recall past sessions | `load_memory` (requires a `MemoryService` on the Runner — see Day 09) |
| You have a REST API with an OpenAPI spec | `OpenApiToolset` |
| You want sandboxed code execution | `BuiltInCodeExecutor` |
| You want a private corpus search | `VertexAiSearchTool` or `DiscoveryEngineSearchTool` |

Most production agents mix three or four of these. A typical customer-support stack: `google_search` for recall notices, `McpToolset` for the internal ticketing system (exposed via MCP), `load_memory` for "what did we discuss last week", and an `AgentTool` wrapping a specialist "billing explain" agent.

sections.title: 6. Four Progressive Examples
sections.body:
Today's examples scale from a 20-line `AgentTool` demo to a real Google Search grounding agent. By Example 4 you will have run an agent that grounds its answers on the live web in under a minute of setup.

1. **Example 1** — AgentTool: parent delegates summarization to a child agent
2. **Example 2** — Local filesystem MCP via stdio (npx server)
3. **Example 3** — Remote Google Maps MCP via streamable HTTP
4. **Example 4** — google_search grounding for current events

Example 1: AgentTool — Parent Delegates Summarization

A parent agent uses a child summarizer agent as a tool; control returns to the parent.

We build two agents. `summarizer` is a focused single-purpose agent — give it text, get back three bullet points. `parent_agent` is a general assistant whose instruction tells it to delegate any "summarize this" request to the summarizer via `AgentTool`.

The key construction is `AgentTool(agent=summarizer, skip_summarization=True)`. `skip_summarization=True` is important here: the parent should treat the child's three bullets as final, not run another LLM pass to "summarize the summary." Without it, you double your LLM cost and risk garbling the output.

Watch what happens in the simulated run: the user asks the parent to summarize a long paragraph, the parent's LLM emits a `function_call` to `summarizer`, the child runs end-to-end and returns its bullets as the function response, and the parent's LLM then produces its own final response that incorporates (or simply echoes) those bullets. The parent stays in charge the whole time — exactly the AgentTool contract.

```python
# agent.py — Example 1: AgentTool delegation
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.tools.agent_tool import AgentTool

# Child agent — focused, single-purpose.
# Note: no tools, no output_schema, just a crisp instruction.
summarizer = Agent(
    name="summarizer",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Summarizes text into exactly three bullet points.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a summarizer. The user will paste text. "
        "Respond with exactly three bullet points (use '- '), "
        "each no longer than 20 words. No preamble, no closing."
    ),
    generate_content_config={"temperature": 0.2, "max_output_tokens": 200},
)

# Parent agent — uses the summarizer as a tool.
# When the user asks to summarize, the LLM will call summarizer().
# When the user asks anything else, the parent answers directly.
root_agent = Agent(
    name="parent_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="A helpful assistant that can summarize text via a specialist sub-agent.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a helpful assistant. When the user asks you to summarize text, "
        "delegate to the 'summarizer' tool — pass the text to summarize as the "
        "argument. Otherwise, answer normally.\n"
        "After receiving the summarizer's output, you may add a one-line lead-in "
        "like 'Here are the key points:' but do NOT rephrase the bullets."
    ),
    tools=[
        AgentTool(
            agent=summarizer,
            skip_summarization=True,   # child output is final
            include_plugins=True,       # default — child inherits parent plugins
        ),
    ],
)

print(f"Parent agent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"  Tools: {[t.name for t in root_agent.tools]}  (one AgentTool wrapping 'summarizer')")
print(f"  summarizer model: {summarizer.model}")
```

**Output**

```text
Parent agent: parent_agent
  Tools: ['summarizer']  (one AgentTool wrapping 'summarizer')
  summarizer model: gemini-2.0-flash
```

```python
# Run the agent
import os
os.environ["GOOGLE_API_KEY"] = "YOUR_GEMINI_API_KEY"

# !adk run my_first_agent
```

**Output**

```text
Welcome to ADK! You are now interacting with parent_agent.

>>> Please summarize this:
    The Model Context Protocol is an open JSON-RPC standard that lets
    LLMs discover and invoke external tools. It was introduced by
    Anthropic in late 2024 and has since been adopted by every major
    agent framework, including Google's ADK. MCP servers expose tools,
    resources, and prompts; clients (your agent) call them over either
    stdio (for local subprocesses) or streamable HTTP (for remote).

[parent_agent] calling tool: summarizer(text='The Model Context Protocol is ...')
[summarizer] running with model gemini-2.0-flash...
[summarizer] final response:
  - MCP is an open JSON-RPC standard for LLM tool discovery.
  - Introduced by Anthropic in late 2024, now widely adopted.
  - Supports stdio and streamable HTTP transports.

Here are the key points:
  - MCP is an open JSON-RPC standard for LLM tool discovery.
  - Introduced by Anthropic in late 2024, now widely adopted.
  - Supports stdio and streamable HTTP transports.
```

💡 Key Concept

Notice the parent *did not* rephrase the bullets. That is the `skip_summarization=True` flag working as advertised: the parent's LLM sees the three bullets as a tool result, prepends "Here are the key points:", and produces its final response — one extra LLM call only, not two.

Example 2: Local Filesystem MCP via StdioConnectionParams

Spawn the official @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem subprocess and give your agent file tools.

The MCP ecosystem ships a reference filesystem server at `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` (npm package). It exposes `list_directory`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `get_file_info`, and friends — all driven by an `npx` subprocess.

To consume it from ADK: import `StdioServerParameters` from the `mcp` package, wrap it in ADK's `StdioConnectionParams`, and pass that to `McpToolset`. The MCP session is opened lazily — the first time the Runner calls `get_tools()`, ADK spawns the subprocess, lists tools, and injects them into the agent's toolset.

The `tool_filter` parameter is your friend. The filesystem server exposes ~8 tools; if your agent only needs to read files, whitelist `["list_directory", "read_file", "get_file_info"]` and the other 5 never reach the LLM's context window. This is the single biggest lever for keeping tool-selection accuracy high.

One gotcha: the path argument to `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem` must be **absolute**. Relative paths silently fail because the npx subprocess's working directory is not your project's.

```python
# agent.py — Example 2: Local filesystem MCP via stdio
import os
from mcp import StdioServerParameters
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool import McpToolset
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.mcp_session_manager import StdioConnectionParams

# Absolute path to the folder the agent may read/write.
# The server enforces this sandbox — the agent cannot escape it.
SANDBOX_DIR = os.path.abspath("./workspace")

# Build the MCP toolset. No I/O happens yet — the subprocess is
# spawned lazily on the first Runner.run_async() call.
filesystem_toolset = McpToolset(
    connection_params=StdioConnectionParams(
        server_params=StdioServerParameters(
            command="npx",
            args=[
                "-y",                                    # auto-install
                "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem",
                SANDBOX_DIR,                             # MUST be absolute
            ],
        ),
    ),
    # Whitelist only the tools we actually want the LLM to see.
    # Without this filter, the agent would also see write_file,
    # move_file, search_files, etc. — more rope to hang itself.
    tool_filter=["list_directory", "read_file", "get_file_info"],
)

root_agent = Agent(
    name="filesystem_assistant",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Reads files and lists directories in a sandboxed workspace.",
    instruction=(
        "You help the user explore files. Use 'list_directory' to show "
        "the contents of a path (use '.' for the workspace root) and "
        "'read_file' to display a file's text content. Always show full "
        "paths. If a path doesn't exist, say so — do not invent contents."
    ),
    tools=[filesystem_toolset],
)

print(f"Agent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"Sandbox: {SANDBOX_DIR}")
print(f"Toolset: {type(filesystem_toolset).__name__} (stdio transport)")
print(f"Filter: list_directory, read_file, get_file_info")
print("(MCP subprocess will spawn on first run_async() call)")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent: filesystem_assistant
Sandbox: /home/z/my-project/workspace
Toolset: McpToolset (stdio transport)
Filter: list_directory, read_file, get_file_info
(MCP subprocess will spawn on first run_async() call)
```

```python
# Run the agent — note the first call is slower (npx subprocess spawns)
# !adk run my_first_agent
```

**Output**

```text

>>> What files are in the workspace?
[McpToolset] spawning: npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem /home/z/my-project/workspace
[McpToolset] MCP session established; 3 tools available after filter
[filesystem_assistant] calling tool: list_directory(path='.')
  tool result: ['notes.md', 'draft.txt', 'todos.json']

The workspace contains three files:
  - notes.md

Here is the content of draft.txt:
```

🚀 Pro Tip

You can inspect the *full* list of tools an MCP server exposes by calling `await toolset.get_tools()` directly after construction — useful when you are deciding what to put in `tool_filter`. Each tool is a `FunctionTool` instance with `.name`, `.description`, and a Pydantic args schema auto-generated from the MCP server's JSON schema.

Example 3: Remote Google Maps MCP via StreamableHTTPConnectionParams

Connect to the hosted Google Maps Grounding Lite MCP server over HTTP.

The Google Maps team publishes a hosted MCP server at `https://mapstools.googleapis.com/mcp`. It exposes tools for geocoding, place search, directions, distance matrix, elevation, and timezone — all grounded on Google's live map data.

Authenticating is as simple as sending your Maps API key in the `X-Goog-Api-Key` header. The `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream` header tells the server you support streaming responses (MCP's preferred transport for long-running tools like directions). Streamable HTTP keeps the connection open for server-to-client messages, which is how MCP supports `elicitation_callback` flows in v2.7.0.

Notice the structural similarity to Example 2: same `McpToolset` class, same `tools=[toolset]` placement on the agent. The only difference is `StreamableHTTPConnectionParams` instead of `StdioConnectionParams`. Your agent code is transport-agnostic — you can swap a local npx server for a remote HTTP server (or vice versa) by changing three lines.

```python
# agent.py — Example 3: Remote Google Maps MCP via streamable HTTP
import os
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool import McpToolset
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.mcp_session_manager import (
    StreamableHTTPConnectionParams,
)

# Get your Maps API key from https://console.cloud.google.com/google/maps-apis
GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY = os.environ.get("GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY", "<your-maps-key>")

maps_toolset = McpToolset(
    connection_params=StreamableHTTPConnectionParams(
        url="https://mapstools.googleapis.com/mcp",
        headers={
            "X-Goog-Api-Key": GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY,
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
            # Accept both single-shot JSON and SSE streaming so the
            # server can pick whichever transport fits each tool.
            "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream",
        },
    ),
    # Filter to the tools we use — maps exposes ~12, we want 4.
    tool_filter=[
        "maps_geocode",        # address → lat/long
        "maps_search_places",  # text query → places
        "maps_directions",     # route between waypoints
        "maps_distance_matrix",  # many-to-many distances
    ],
)

root_agent = Agent(
    name="maps_assistant",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Plans trips and routes using live Google Maps data.",
    instruction=(
        "You help users plan travel using Google Maps. Use 'maps_search_places' "
        "to find specific venues, 'maps_directions' to plan routes, and "
        "'maps_distance_matrix' to compare options. Always show distances in km "
        "and durations in hours/minutes. If a place name is ambiguous, ask."
    ),
    tools=[maps_toolset],
)

print(f"Agent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"MCP endpoint: https://mapstools.googleapis.com/mcp")
print(f"Transport: streamable HTTP (SSE-capable)")
print(f"Whitelisted tools: 4 (geocode, search_places, directions, distance_matrix)")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent: maps_assistant
MCP endpoint: https://mapstools.googleapis.com/mcp
Transport: streamable HTTP (SSE-capable)
Whitelisted tools: 4 (geocode, search_places, directions, distance_matrix)
```

```python
# Run the agent
# export GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY="..."
# !adk run my_first_agent
```

**Output**

```text
Welcome to ADK! You are now interacting with maps_assistant.

>>> How long does it take to drive from San Francisco to Los Angeles?
[McpToolset] connecting to https://mapstools.googleapis.com/mcp ...
[McpToolset] MCP session established; 4 tools available
[maps_assistant] calling tool: maps_geocode(address='San Francisco, CA')
  → {'lat': 37.7749, 'lng': -122.4194}
[maps_assistant] calling tool: maps_geocode(address='Los Angeles, CA')
  → {'lat': 34.0522, 'lng': -118.2437}
[maps_assistant] calling tool: maps_directions(origin=..., destination=...)
  → {'distance_km': 616, 'duration_minutes': 374, 'route': 'I-5 S'}

Driving from San Francisco to Los Angeles takes about 6 hours 14 minutes
via I-5 S, covering roughly 616 km. Leave before 7am to avoid LA rush hour.
```

💡 Key Concept

The geocoding, directions, and distance-matrix calls happened inside the MCP server — your agent never imported `googlemaps` or wrote a `requests.get(...)`. The MCP protocol abstracted all of that away. This is the value proposition: **any MCP server, any transport, one client class**.

Example 4: google_search Grounding — Live Web in One Line

Add the `google_search` pre-built tool to ground agent responses on the live web.

Sometimes you do not need MCP, an OpenAPI spec, or even a custom function — you just need current information. Stock prices, news, sports scores, software release notes, weather alerts. For all of these, `google_search` is the right tool.

Adding `google_search` to an agent's `tools` list enables Google Search grounding on the Gemini API. The LLM decides when to search (typically for any factual question that might have changed since its training cutoff), runs the search, and incorporates the results into its response. The grounding metadata — search queries used, source URLs, supporting snippets — comes back as a `grounding_metadata` field on the response, which you can render as inline citations in your UI.

**What makes this special:** no API key beyond your existing Gemini key. No MCP subprocess. No OpenAPI spec. No HTTP client. Just `from google.adk.tools import google_search` and add it to the list. It is the lowest-effort, highest-impact tool in ADK's catalog.

v2.7.0 added `propagate_grounding_metadata` on `AgentTool` (Day 06 §2.1) — pair that with `google_search` on a child agent to surface the child's citations in the parent's response. We will see that pattern in the exercises.

```python
# agent.py — Example 4: google_search grounding
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.tools import google_search

root_agent = Agent(
    name="current_events_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Answers questions about current events using live Google Search results.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a news and current-events assistant. For any factual question "
        "whose answer may have changed recently (stock prices, election results, "
        "software releases, sports scores, weather warnings), use the 'google_search' "
        "tool to ground your answer.\n"
        "Always cite sources inline as [1], [2], etc., matching the grounding metadata.\n"
        "If the search returns nothing relevant, say so — do not guess."
    ),
    tools=[google_search],
    # generate_content_config is optional but useful here:
    # higher temperature gives more natural phrasing for news summaries.
    generate_content_config={"temperature": 0.4, "max_output_tokens": 400},
)

print(f"Agent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"Tool: google_search (grounding on the live web)")
print(f"Note: grounding metadata returned with every search-grounded response")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent: current_events_agent
Tool: google_search (grounding on the live web)
Note: grounding metadata returned with every search-grounded response
```

```python
# Run the agent
# !adk run my_first_agent
```

**Output**

```text
Welcome to ADK! You are now interacting with current_events_agent.

>>> What is the latest version of Python?
[current_events_agent] invoking google_search(query='latest stable Python version')
  grounding metadata:
    queries: ['latest stable Python version', 'Python 3.13 release date']
    sources: [1] python.org/downloads  [2] dev.to/python/release-notes

The latest stable Python release is Python 3.13.x, which shipped in October
2024 [1]. Key features include a new interactive REPL, experimental free-
threaded build (PEP 703), and the @deprecated decorator (PEP 702) [2].

Sources:
  [1] https://www.python.org/downloads/
  [2] https://dev.to/python/release-notes-python-313
```

🚀 Pro Tip

The grounding metadata is exposed on the `Event` object's `content.parts[0].grounding_metadata` — you can extract it programmatically to build UI components (citation chips, source cards, etc.). The metadata includes the search queries the LLM chose to run, which is gold for debugging "why did it cite this source?" questions.

sections.title: Day 6 Summary
sections.body:
📌 Key Takeaways

- **AgentTool** wraps an agent as a callable tool — control returns to the parent. Use it for focused delegation where the parent needs the child's *output*.

- **sub_agents** transfers control — the child owns the rest of the turn. Use it when the child should take over the conversation.

- **`AgentTool(agent=..., skip_summarization=True, include_plugins=True)` — skip summarization when the child's output is final; include_plugins defaults to True so analytics plugins fire on the child too.**

- **McpToolset** is ADK's bridge to the Model Context Protocol. Same class for stdio (local npx) and streamable-HTTP (remote) transports — only the `connection_params` differ.

- **`tool_filter=['list_directory', 'read_file']` whitelists tools — the single biggest lever for keeping the LLM's tool-selection accurate.**

- **v2.7.0 added `elicitation_callback` on McpToolset and lets the toolset reuse a server's existing tool list (perf win for hot-reload dev loops).**

- **ADK ships a toolbox of pre-built tools: `google_search` (zero-config web grounding), `load_memory`, `load_web_page`, `BuiltInCodeExecutor`, `OpenApiToolset` (any REST API with a spec), `VertexAiSearchTool`, and the now-stable `DataAgentToolset`.**
